grh_8061dff5bbd9f78edb39.title: Abilene
paragraphs: Mayor Joseph McCoy, desperate to restore order to cattle-boom Abilene, hires Civil War veteran and scout James Butler Hickok as marshal after other lawmen have failed. Hickok moves quickly against the violent saloons and crooked gambling, closing the back room at the Bull's Head and making an enemy of proprietor Phil Coe. Coe answers by inflaming the Texas cattlemen against the new 'Yankee' marshal and organizing a mob to run him out of town. Hickok refuses to be driven off, while his allies seek help from the town's farmers, and the confrontation ends in gunfire that shows how difficult it will be to impose law on Abilene's violence.

This [[show|sears-radio-theater|Sears Radio Theater]] broadcast aired on April 23, 1979. It is listed as episode 56 in the archive. [[org|org.8480b75bc0c36e4b|CBS Radio Network]] carried the broadcast. The cast includes Norman Alden, [[person|parley-baer|Parley Baer]], Tom Brown, Fletcher Markle, and Howard Culver. Other credited names include Fletcher Markle as director, Fletcher Markle as producer, Michael Angelela as writer, James Knots as writer, and Lorne Greene as host.
The broadcast is also associated with [[org|org.9b0a0ccffce2f7d3|Sears, Roebuck and Company]].

grh_8096d36365e2a4d33542.title: Johnny Springer
paragraphs: After a hotelkeeper is shot, Britt and the sheriff follow the trail of a notorious fugitive to a young woman named Maria, who has been hiding a man she knows under an alias and expects to marry. The lawmen reveal that her guest is the wanted gunman, already married and accustomed to using women to help him escape. When he turns a gun on Britt and the sheriff, Maria accepts that she has been deceived and kills him with a knife. Britt later argues that her act may have saved their lives, and she appears to come through the legal aftermath safely.

grh_80832af9701c2ab54cb2.title: Nazis Go Underground
paragraphs: A warning-oriented dramatization argues that Nazi power could survive military defeat by moving underground. Staged scenes show German officials planning infiltration, propaganda, sabotage and the placement of loyal personnel inside institutions likely to be used by occupying forces. The broadcast broadens the warning beyond Germany, arguing that fascism thrives wherever fear, racial hatred, poverty and political manipulation are allowed to grow, and concludes that military victory must be followed by dismantling Nazi organization and improving the conditions that make fascism attractive.

Other credited names include Anton M. Leader as director, Ben Kagan as radio adaptor, Clifton Fadiman as host, and Jack Costello as announcer.
The surviving recording runs about 29 minutes. The broadcast is also associated with [[org|org.a811c0d1a6efa194|Johnson's Wax]].
This version dramatizes [[work|work.words.b51a78685280f3c2|Nazis Go Underground]]. Curt Reese is credited as author and Ben Kagan adapted it for radio.

grh_8068deb0f59c673dc876.title: Words at War 43-11-23 (24) Escape from the Balkans
paragraphs: Bulgarian journalist Michael Padev, a correspondent for British newspapers, is arrested after German influence tightens over wartime Bulgaria. Interrogation and torture give way to imprisonment in the Gondavoda camp, where he and fellow prisoners endure disease, deprivation and constant surveillance. Padev helps carry word of the camp to outside contacts and eventually joins an escape attempt using forged papers. After tense checks at the frontier, he reaches Turkey and freedom, while the broadcast links his story to the wider partisan struggle against fascist control of the Balkans.

paragraphs: Through letters to her absent husband, Anne Hilton describes how she and her daughters adjust after he leaves for military service.
